what: Brink’s is the world’s largest cash management company. It moves and stores cash and valuables in armoured trucks and vaults, manages ATMs for banks, and increasingly sells retailers smart safes and services that turn cash in the till into a bank deposit without a trip to the bank.
customers: Banks, retailers, central banks, casinos and jewellers in more than 50 countries.
money: Armoured transport, cash processing, vaulting and global services for precious metals and valuables.
ATM managed services and digital retail solutions
Running ATM networks for banks and recurring-revenue cash automation for retailers.
moat: Route density and trust. Armoured logistics needs vehicles, vaults, licences and insurance in every market, and the company with the densest routes has the lowest cost per stop.
risks: Cash use is declining in many developed economies, shrinking the core market slowly.
The company carries $4.6 billion of debt, and labour-intensive operations face wage pressure.
Currency and political risk in emerging markets, notably Latin America, affect results.
opportunities: ATM managed services and digital retail solutions grow faster and earn steadier, subscription-like revenue.
Banks outsourcing their ATM fleets give Brink’s a growing market as cash use declines.
watch: The share of revenue from ATM managed services and digital retail solutions. It is the part of the business that turns declining cash use from a threat into a growth opportunity.
view: The obvious story about Brink’s is that cash is dying, and the obvious story is too simple. Cash use is falling in rich countries but not disappearing, and the fewer cash transactions there are, the less sense it makes for banks and retailers to run their own cash operations. Brink’s is positioning itself as the company that takes those operations off their hands, which is why revenue has grown from $4.2 billion in 2021 to $5.5 billion over the last twelve months rather than shrinking.

The reported P/E of nearly 30 overstates the valuation; GAAP earnings carry restructuring costs, currency effects and acquisition amortisation. On EV/EBITDA of about 8.7 and 12.6 times free cash flow, the shares are moderately priced for a business with real pricing power in its core routes. The debt of $4.6 billion is substantial but offset partly by $1.7 billion of cash, some of which is tied to operations.

The whole case rests on whether ATM managed services and retail cash automation keep growing fast enough to outweigh decline in traditional armoured transport. If they do, Brink’s becomes a steadier, more recurring business that deserves a higher multiple. If they stall, it is a leveraged company in a shrinking market. Progress so far supports the optimistic version, and the analyst target about 29% above the price suggests the market has not yet fully believed it.
bull: ATM outsourcing and retail cash automation grow fast enough to make the business more recurring, while cost cuts lift margins.
bear: Cash use falls faster than expected, high debt limits flexibility, and labour costs squeeze margins in the traditional route business.
